desc:
The string s contains only '(' and ')'. A string is valid when it is non-empty and well-formed: every '(' is closed by a later ')' and every ')' closes an earlier '('.

Count the substrings of s that are valid. Substrings are contiguous and are counted by their position, so two equal substrings at different places count separately.

For example, "(()())" has 4 valid substrings: "()" twice (at indices 1-2 and 3-4), "()()" and the whole string.
hints: Checking all O(n2) substrings with a counter is correct but slow for n = 10,000 in some languages. Try counting valid substrings by their last character.
A valid substring can only end at a ')'. If that ')' is matched by a stack to an opening bracket at index j, then s[j..i] is valid.

Let dp[i] be the number of valid substrings ending at i. If s[i] matches index j, then dp[i] = 1 + dp[j-1] (with dp[-1] = 0): the pair itself, or the pair preceded by any valid substring that ends right before j. Otherwise dp[i] = 0. The answer is the sum of dp.
editorial: Match brackets with a stack of indices. When a ')' at index i finds an opening bracket at j on the stack, the segment s[j..i] is well-formed. Every valid substring ending at i has this segment as its last primitive piece, preceded by a (possibly empty) valid substring that ends at j - 1. There are dp[j-1] non-empty choices for that prefix plus the empty one, so dp[i] = dp[j-1] + 1.

A ')' with an empty stack can never be part of a valid substring, and neither can any substring crossing it, which is handled automatically: nothing matches across it, so dp stays 0 there and the stack is empty as well. Adding all dp[i] gives the answer in O(n) time and O(n) space. The result is at most about n2/8, which fits easily in 32 bits.
